1.pericope_label: Amalek sacks Ziklag in David’s absence, and his own men speak of stoning him

schools.summary: Henry finds two corrections in the raid: the cruelty of Saul’s pity in sparing the Amalekites, since had he destroyed them as he ought these would not have been in being to do the mischief, and a rebuke to David for his forwardness to march with the Philistines, for when we go abroad in the way of our duty we may hope God will keep our families in our absence, but not otherwise. On the sparing of the captives he presses hardest of all: when David invaded Amalek he put all to the sword, and no reason can be given why they did not retaliate in kind but that God restrained them, who says to the fury of the cruellest men, Hitherto shalt thou come and no further; whether they were kept for triumph, sale or slavery, God designed to use Amalek for the correction and not the destruction of the house of David. On the mutiny he gives two causes, that the men blamed him for provoking Amalek and leaving Ziklag ungarrisoned, and that they now despaired of the preferment they had promised themselves, hoping ere this to have been all princes and finding themselves all beggars. On the last clause he sets David against them: the soul of the people was bitter and their impatience added wormwood to the affliction, but while they gave liberty to their passions he set his graces on work, so that when he was at his wits’ end he was not at his faith’s end.

Gill reckons the march home from the Philistine camp at eighty-eight miles, which makes three days no wonder, and attributes David’s particular distress to the loss of his two wives together with the mutiny of his men.

Keil and Delitzsch are explicit that the third day is reckoned from David’s dismissal by Achish and not from his leaving Ziklag, and they set out the opening verses as one long period whose apodosis does not arrive until the weeping. On the mutiny they say the people sought the occasion of the calamity in his connection with Achish, which many of his adherents had very probably disliked. Ellicott adds the geography, that the dismissal can hardly have happened at Shunem, some ninety miles off, so the scene must have fallen somewhere in Philistia after the whole force had gathered. He explains the sparing of the captives commercially, women and children having a marketable value and being carried off for sale, probably into Egypt, with which the Amalekites as neighbours had constant dealings; and he sharpens the mutiny into the bitter degradation of having marched against their own countrymen under the banner of Gath, so that pent-up fury found its vent. On the closing clause he makes the encouragement prayer, David throwing himself on the mercy of the God who had chosen him, and sets against it the contrast that at about the same hour Saul, alone and distrustful, fought and fell on the bloody day of Gilboa.

Clarke cites Calmet for more than thirty leagues between Aphek and Ziklag, and reads the raiders as a travelling predatory horde who had plainly not heard what David had done to their tribe, or they would have slain every soul they found. On the mutiny he reads the men’s temper rather than their grievance: David had done much to civilise them, yet here is their unruly and ferocious spirit, and yet they strongly felt the ties of natural affection and grieved every man for his sons and daughters. He grounds David’s encouragement in a clear conscience, this evil having come through neither his neglect nor his folly. Wesley lists the counts against David flatly — coming to Ziklag at first, provoking the Amalekites, marching away with Achish, and leaving the families unguarded.

7.pericope_label: David calls for the ephod, enquires of the LORD, and is guided by an abandoned Egyptian slave

schools.summary: Henry holds that if David had priest and ephod with him in the Philistine camp it was a great neglect not to have enquired about his engagement to Achish, perhaps being ashamed to own his religion so far among the uncircumcised; he now apprehends the trouble was brought to correct that oversight, so the first thing he does is call for the ephod, and it is well if we get this good by our afflictions, to be reminded of neglected duties. On the two hundred left at the brook he sees both a trial of David’s faith, whether he could go on depending on the word of God when a third of his men failed him, and an instance of his tenderness in not urging them beyond their strength, the Son of David likewise considering the frame of followers who are not all alike vigorous, for where we are weak there he is kind. On the abandoned slave he is sharpest: that master has the spirit of an Amalekite and not of an Israelite who can use a servant worse than a beast, and the tender mercies of the wicked are cruel; justly did Providence make this abused servant the instrument of a whole army’s destruction, for God hears the cry of oppressed servants. He also reads the lad’s request as evidence of how binding he thought an oath.

Gill makes the pursuit itself an act of faith, four hundred being a small number against an enemy whose strength David did not know, and notes that as many afterwards escaped on camels as he had men with him.

Ellicott presses the neglect furthest: through all the wanderings we hear nothing of prayer or of consulting the Urim, and David seems to have determined the Philistine sojourn entirely of himself, one unbroken series of sin and calamity being the result. He then defends the Urim as the actual medium of the answer, against modern commentators who prefer to disbelieve in any response through it, passing the transaction over or assuming some inspiration came to the high priest when vested; the plain sense of the frequent references is that the divine will was made known through it, and the case of Saul distinguishes being answered by Urim from a dream, a vision or a prophet. He grants the Talmudic traditions are in places fanciful, yet calls it arbitrary to reject the ancient belief of the Hebrew race about the sacred gems for a reading that fits the text lamely. He also takes the six hundred for the veteran band whose speed and endurance David could depend on, and calls the desertion of the sick slave a needless barbarity given the camels in their train. Keil and Delitzsch keep to the relief itself, the slice of fig-cake and the raisin-cakes, after which the man’s spirit of life returned to him.

Wesley has David sensible of his former error, necessity bringing him to his duty and his duty meeting with success; and he attends to the manner of the answer rather than its medium, since formerly God answered slowly and gradually but now speedily and at once because the business required haste, so gracious is he that he considers even the degree of our necessities. With Gill he makes the pursuit an act of faith. On the slave he finds the providence further back still, that the lad was not of the cursed race appointed to destruction but an Egyptian who might be spared, so that there is no fighting against God, who can make the smallest accidents serviceable to the greatest effects. Clarke calls the desertion inhuman when they had asses enough, says God visited it upon them, and notes that the two hundred at the brook were appointed to guard the baggage.

positions.view: Yes — the plain sense of the references, and it is arbitrary to reject the ancient Hebrew belief about the gems

16.pericope_label: Amalek found feasting and spread abroad, cut off from twilight to evening, and all the spoil recovered

schools.summary: Henry draws the moral twice over: sinners are nearest to ruin when they cry peace and safety and put the evil day far from them, and nothing gives our spiritual enemies more advantage than sensuality, eating and drinking and dancing having been the soft and pleasant way in which many have gone down to the congregation of the dead; so the triumphing of the wicked is short, and wrath comes on them, as on Belshazzar, in the midst of their jollity. He supposes the revelry was held in honour of their idol-gods, to whom they gave the praise of their success, and reads the whole recovery as a resemblance to the Son of David, who took the prey from the mighty and led captivity captive. On the distribution of the drovers’ cry he marks the turn in the men, that those who lately spoke of stoning David now magnify him because they got by him more than they had lost, so that the world and its sentiments are governed by interest.

Gill lays out the twilight question without deciding it: some take the morning, so that David came by night, let them alone till they were drunk and asleep, and fell on them early, as Josephus relates it; others the evening, with the Targum; and some read the morrow as following two evenings, which would carry the slaughter into a third day. He also notes that not one captive, small or great, was lacking in the recovery.

Keil and Delitzsch settle the twilight lexically for the evening, holding that the word means the evening twilight here and not the dawn, a sense not even sustained by the one passage urged for it. On the drovers’ cry they call the verse obscure and resolve it by distinguishing the herds, the Amalekites’ own sheep and oxen being driven in front of the cattle recovered from them, so that the foremost were called David’s booty. Ellicott reports their reading of the twilight but prefers Bishop Hervey’s against it, that the contrast drawn between twilight and evening rather suggests the morning: David arrived at night, deferred the attack till dawn when they would still be sleeping off the debauch, and was then held all day by their numbers. He imagines the assault from the other side, the veterans looking on the revel and remembering whose homes had been laid waste to furnish the spoil Amalek was rejoicing over, then falling on the robbers with a fury that carried them against far greater numbers. On the drovers’ cry he reaches the same reading as Keil and Delitzsch, blames the italicised word in the English for obscuring it, and finds David’s motive in choosing flocks and herds, for warriors the least desirable share, plain from what he does with them next.

Clarke twice declines to let the slaughter be justified too easily. That these Amalekites were enemies of the Philistines is evident, he grants, but it does not follow that the people David destroyed were enemies too, which has been too hastily assumed by Dr Chandler and others the better to vindicate David’s character; and though Amalek was a proscribed nation, so that David has been supposed in extirpating them to fulfil the express will of God, that depends on whether he had an express commission from God himself, as Saul had. Wesley argues for the evening twilight on two grounds, that feasting and dancing are evening work and that darkness kept the fewness of David’s force from being seen, and he accounts for the Amalekites’ security circumstantially: they were almost home, both armies were engaged elsewhere, and David they believed was with them, so they had no visible cause of danger and were then nearest destruction. With Henry he marks the turn in the men who had lately spoken of stoning David.

21.pericope_label: The two hundred at the brook are met, the men of Belial would defraud them, and David makes it a statute

schools.summary: Henry notes that the two hundred came out to congratulate a success they could not contribute to, since we should rejoice in a good work done though Providence has laid us aside, and that David, far from upbraiding their weakness, asked them of peace, having left them faint and unwell, or bade them be of good cheer and lose nothing by staying behind, which is what they seemed afraid of. He is harshest on the objectors: probably the same men who had spoken of stoning David now spoke of defrauding their brethren, and a while ago they would gladly have given half their own to recover the other half, yet having all their own they are not content without their brethren’s too, so soon do men forget their low estate; to return the wives and children without the goods was to give them the mouths without the meat, and those are men of Belial indeed who delight in putting hardships on their brethren and care not who is starved so they may be fed to the full. He gives David’s grounds as gratitude and justice: the spoil is what God has given, to be used under his direction, and God’s mercy to us should make us merciful to one another; while in justice the two hundred stayed behind for want of strength and not of good-will, had done their part in former actions, and even now did good service guarding what somebody had to guard, for every post of service is not alike a post of honour, yet those serviceable in a meaner station ought to share, as every member of the body has its use and so its share of the nourishment. He calls the rule a statute of distributions of the first year of David’s reign, and points to Abraham quitting his title to the spoils of Sodom by the law of war.

Gill calls the objectors ill-natured and covetous, and reads their answer as implying that the two hundred had asked for a share. He has David deal gently while still keeping up his dignity as general. On the statute he reports that the Hebrew reads upwards, of old, so that Jarchi makes it a rule already of Abraham’s day from which David learnt it, though Josephus is express that the law obtained from David’s own time.

Ellicott has David salute the two hundred with all kindly courtesy, and the camp’s harmony broken immediately after. He traces the ordinance forward, the decision remaining in force until the Maccabees, and sets beside it the scene in Polybius where Scipio, after taking Nova Carthago, divided the spoil equally among the troops engaged, the reserves, the sick, and those detached on special service. Keil and Delitzsch keep to the grammar, taking the particle for the accusative sign and not the preposition, and one written form for a copyist’s error.

Clarke glosses the phrase for men of Belial as the common expression for the sour, the rugged, the severe, the idle and the profane; he takes the words unto this day for another indication that the book was composed long after the events it records. Wesley remarks with Henry and Gill on the address, that David overruled the objectors but called them brethren and owned them as fellow-soldiers, managing his authority with sweetness; and on the statute he cites the same Roman practice Ellicott does, giving the reason that the reserve shares the hazard, stands ready for a retreat, and is in actual service where its general placed it.

26.pericope_label: From Ziklag David sends portions of the spoil to the elders of Judah and every place he had haunted

schools.summary: Henry divides the act three ways. There is generosity, since David aimed not to enrich himself but to serve his country, and God afterwards enriched him and set him to rule the country he had served. There is piety, for he calls the gift a blessing, no present being a comfort to our friends but as God’s blessing makes it so, which intimates that his prayers went with it; and he sends it from the spoil of the enemies of the Lord, so calling them rather than his own enemies, that the receivers might rejoice in the victory for the Lord’s sake. And there is policy, to engage his countrymen to appear for him at an accession he now saw at hand, since a man’s gift makes room for him, munificence recommending a man more than magnificence. He notices too who got nothing, the Ziphites having none of these presents, nor the men of Keilah, which shows that though he was such a saint as not to revenge affronts he was not such a fool as not to take notice of them. On the list he makes the name of the first place the point rather than its site, Bethel signifying the house of God and being served first for its name’s sake, or else what is meant is wherever the ark then was, and thither David sent the first and best, for the sake of him who is first and best; and he reads Hebron’s coming last as the residuum being the largest share, David having an eye already on the place as fittest for his head-quarters.

Gill rejects the Bethel of Benjamin for Kirjathjearim, called Bethel because the ark was there. On Aroer he refuses the identification beyond Jordan outright, on the ground that David is never said to have been there, so that some city of the name in Judah must be meant.

Keil and Delitzsch press the policy of the gifts, which could not fail to make these elders well disposed and so to ease David’s recognition as king after Saul’s death, which followed immediately; some of the places, they add, may themselves have been plundered, Amalek having invaded the Negeb of Judah. They rule out the famous Bethel for the first name on the list. Ellicott agrees the towns must be those where David and his followers had been kindly received in the long wanderings, and takes the first name for Bethuel or Bethul in Simeon, noting that the Greek reads another name altogether. On Aroer he describes colossal ruins south of Hebron without arguing the point. He closes with an observation he credits to Bishop Hervey, that it is a remarkable proof of David’s grateful nature and his fidelity to early friendships that among the men he employed in offices of trust at the height of his power we find so many inhabitants of these obscure places — Ezri the son of Shemei the Ramathite, Zabdi the Shiphmite and many besides, the friends of his youth — and he traces two of them himself, taking the officer over the vineyards for a native of Ramah of the South and the keeper of the cellars for a man of Siphmoth.

Wesley puts the motive most briefly, partly in gratitude for former favours and partly in policy, to engage their affections. Clarke has the recipients for the people among whom David sojourned in exile, who had given him shelter and protection, so that gratitude required the presents; he places the first name on the list in Ephraim, and puts Aroer beyond Jordan on the Arnon in the tribe of Gad.
